cf.title: Windows relation extension failure at 2GB and 4GB

input.subject: [Patch] Windows relation extension failure at 2GB and 4GB

verdict_reasoning: The I/O fix is committed to HEAD and no one disputes the goal. What remains is the test module and the v6 meson.build change, and all three surviving objections are fixable level 2 points. standards-compat-1 is the strongest: v6 removes the meson segment size check while other code still uses off_t. maintenance-fit-2 and maintenance-fit-3 repeat requests from the engaged committer that v6 does not yet meet.

brief.title: Use pgoff_t in the file I/O layer so Windows files can exceed 2GB
brief.problem: On Windows with MSVC, off_t is 32 bits, so relation files built with a segment size above 1GB fail to extend at 2GB with "could not extend file: Invalid argument". Past the 2GB fix, the Windows pg_pwrite()/pg_pread() wrap at 4GB because they never set OffsetHigh. This affects only people who build with a larger segment size, which the author says is rare.
brief.proposed_design: The patch replaces off_t with pgoff_t in fd.c, md.c, pg_iovec.h, file_utils.c and their headers, and sets both Offset and OffsetHigh in the Windows OVERLAPPED wrappers. v6 adds a test module, test_large_files, which writes and reads a sparse temporary file at 4GB+1 through the VFD layer and checks FileSize(). v6 also touches the top-level meson.build.
user_visible_surface: C API: File* functions in fd.h such as FileSize() and FileTruncate() take or return pgoff_t instead of off_t.
C API: pg_preadv(), pg_pwritev(), pg_pread(), pg_pwrite() and pg_pwrite_zeros() take pgoff_t offsets.
New test module test_large_files with SQL functions test_large_files_offset_size() and test_large_files_test_4gb_boundary().
Build: meson check that rejects a segment size of 2GB or more when off_t is under 8 bytes, committed and backpatched to v16 separately.
author_claims: Both bugs reproduce reliably with segsize=8, failing at exactly 2GB and then at exactly 4GB.
The change is safe on Unix because pgoff_t equals off_t there, so only Windows behavior changes.
The test at 4GB+1 catches both bugs, while a test at 2GB+1 would miss the OffsetHigh bug.
The test completes in seconds on most platforms.
brief.thread_state: Michael Paquier committed the meson segment size check down to v16 and the I/O routine changes to HEAD; the open part is the test module. In the last message, Michael asks for modular SQL wrappers around File* functions and a .gitignore, questions the pgoff_t size check, and opposes dropping the meson check while buffile.c still uses off_t.
unclear: The v6 commit message describes the I/O fix, but its file list shows only meson.build and the test module, so the patch scope does not match its message.
The patch does not say what it changes in meson.build, and whether it removes the large-file segment size check.
No version after v6 is visible, and the material does not show if the author accepted the File* wrapper design.
The patch does not add a PG_TEST_EXTRA gate, which Michael suggested for machines with little disk space.
The thread does not say when buffile.c and the other off_t users will be converted.

prior_attempts.title: Windows pg_basebackup unable to create >2GB pg_wal.tar tarballs ("could not close file: Invalid argument" when creating pg_wal.tar of size ~ 2^31 bytes)
prior_attempts.reason: The visible messages do not show why. The last message discusses how to back-patch the fix, including an ftruncate() replacement, and nobody objects to it. The entry was withdrawn three days later, and no message gives a reason.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1 fixed 32-bit off_t in frontend tar writing (lseek, ftruncate) for pg_basebackup. This proposal fixes the backend fd.c and md.c layer and the OVERLAPPED wrappers. P1 was withdrawn with no recorded reason, so no objection carries over.

prior_attempts.title: Large files for relations
prior_attempts.quote: If I run it with 64kB, the test pgbench/001_pgbench_with_server fails consistently, so it seems there is still a gap somewhere.
prior_attempts.reason: The author dropped the first plan because segmented mode cannot be removed: ext4 limits files to 16TB, and whole-relation files make file-level backups coarser. The --rel-segsize patch then missed v17 over open problems with incremental backup: pg_combinebasebackup and the segment size, and memory use in basebackup_incremental.c that grows with segment size. Peter Eisentraut's May 2024 review found that the patch needed a rebase and that pgbench/001_pgbench_with_server fails with a 64kB segment size. No revised patch appears in the visible messages.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P2 aimed at a per-cluster segment size set at initdb and stalled on incremental backup. This proposal keeps the compile-time segment size and only makes offsets 64-bit on Windows, so P2's recorded problems do not apply.

objections.title: v6 removes the meson segment size check before all relation-file paths are converted
objections.failure_scenario: A packager builds with MSVC and -Dsegsize=4, which v6 lets meson accept. The server extends relation files past 2GB, but CREATE DATABASE with file copy, pg_rewind or pg_basebackup handles those files through code that still uses off_t. The failure shows up later, during a copy, rewind or backup.
objections.argument: Message #28 quotes v6 removing the `cc.sizeof('off_t') < 8` check from meson.build. The commit message does not mention this change. The thread names off_t users that remain: buffile.c (message #30), and copydir.c and pg_rewind's libpq_source.c and filemap.c (message #2). configure keeps its own check, so after v6 the two build systems would accept different segment sizes for the same compiler.
objections.author_must_show: Which code paths that read, copy or back up relation segment files still use off_t, and can the meson check stay until all of them use pgoff_t?

critic.reasoning: Message #28 quotes the v6 hunk that removes the check, and messages #2 and #30 name off_t users that remain. No visible reply from the author addresses this, and keeping the check is a small change.

objections.title: A 4GB sparse-file test runs in every check with no opt-in gate
objections.failure_scenario: A buildfarm animal or developer runs make check on a filesystem without sparse file support, or on a small SD card. The test writes past 4GB, so the run fills the disk or becomes very slow. Everyone who runs check pays this cost, but only MSVC builds with a large segment size gain anything.
objections.argument: In message #24, Michael proposed a new PG_TEST_EXTRA value for this reason. The v6 README mentions only NO_INSTALLCHECK and claims the test completes in seconds "on most platforms". Sparse files are a property of the filesystem, and nothing checks for them before the test writes past 4GB. Both the README and message #26 frame the gate as optional.
objections.author_must_show: What happens to make check on a filesystem without sparse files, and why should the test not be gated by PG_TEST_EXTRA?

critic.reasoning: Message #24 asks for a PG_TEST_EXTRA gate and v6 sets only NO_INSTALLCHECK. Message #27 dropped FSCTL_SET_SPARSE, so the write at 4GB+1 may allocate real disk space on NTFS and on filesystems without sparse files.

objections.title: Test module is a single fixed scenario, not reusable File* wrappers
objections.failure_scenario: The off_t conversion of buffile.c or pg_rewind later needs a test of its own. The hard-coded test_large_files_test_4gb_boundary() cannot express it, so a second module or another fixed C function gets added. The tree then holds several narrow I/O test modules for one problem.
objections.argument: Michael asked in message #9 and again in message #28 for thin SQL wrappers around File* functions that take bytea and an offset. The v6 test is one C function that runs a fixed sequence. It also checks sizeof(pgoff_t), which is 8 bytes in every build (message #28), so that check can never skip anything. No later version shows the requested design.
objections.author_must_show: Can the module expose open, write, read and size wrappers that take an offset and bytea, so that later off_t conversions reuse it?

critic.reasoning: The test module is the open part of the patch, and the engaged committer asks for modular File* wrappers in message #28, with no visible reply. The sizeof(pgoff_t) check is always true, as message #28 says.

refuted.title: Dropping the meson segment size check exposes pg_rewind and backup paths
refuted.failure_scenario: A packager builds HEAD on Windows with MSVC and -Dsegsize=8, which the build would accept once the check is gone. Relation segments then grow past 4GB. After a failover, pg_rewind copies changed ranges of such a segment through code that message #2 reports as still using off_t, and the rewound standby can hold wrong data that shows up only when it is queried.
refuted.argument: The v6 diff quoted in message #28 removes the meson check that rejects a segment size of 2GB or more when off_t is under 8 bytes. v6 converts only fd.c, md.c and the pread/pwrite wrappers, and message #2 lists pg_rewind (libpq_source.c, filemap.c), copydir.c and buffile.c as unconverted. Michael objects in message #28 but cites only buffile.c. Tools that copy relation files between nodes are the larger risk, because a wrong offset there writes bad data instead of raising an error.
refuted.author_must_show: Can the meson check stay until every path that reads or writes relation segments, including pg_rewind and base backup, uses pgoff_t?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. The claim that pg_rewind writes wrong data without an error goes beyond message #2, which says only that it "seems also broken".

refuted.title: v6 drops the meson segment size check while buffile.c still uses off_t
refuted.failure_scenario: A packager builds HEAD with MSVC and -Dsegsize=4, which meson now accepts. Relation files work, but code still using off_t, such as buffile.c and copydir.c, can truncate offsets past 2GB. The packager finds out from a runtime error or a wrong offset, with no build error to warn them.
refuted.argument: Message #28 shows v6 deleting the check that Michael backpatched to v16 in message #19, and Michael objects that much of the tree still uses off_t (messages #28, #30). Message #2 lists further off_t users, including copydir.c and pg_rewind. Removing the check makes the build trust a conversion that is only partly done. If anyone forgets one of the remaining off_t sites, nothing fails loudly.
refuted.author_must_show: Which remaining off_t users can see offsets above 2GB with a larger segment size, and are they all converted before the meson check is removed?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which covers the same removed check and the same remaining off_t users.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: File* functions in fd.h and pg_pread(), pg_pwrite(), pg_preadv(), pg_pwritev() change their offset type from off_t to pgoff_t.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The signature changes went to HEAD only because of ABI risk; only the meson segment size check was backpatched to v16.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: A new test module, test_large_files, and an off_t conversion that is only partly done across the tree.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: The patch changes offset types in fd.c, md.c and the pread/pwrite wrappers, which every relation read and write uses.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Does v6 remove the meson check that rejects a segment size of 2GB or more when off_t is under 8 bytes, and if so, why?
Which code paths that read, copy or back up relation segment files still use off_t, and when will they move to pgoff_t?
What happens to make check on a filesystem without sparse files, and why is the test not gated by a PG_TEST_EXTRA value?
Can the module expose open, write, read and size wrappers that take an offset and bytea, as message #28 asks?
Why does the v6 commit message describe the I/O fix when its file list holds only meson.build and the test module?

committability.owner_note: Michael Paquier committed the meson check and the I/O changes and reviews the test module in message #28. The owner needs to know the Windows port and the fd.c layer.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a test module that writes past 4GB on every buildfarm animal, and for the meson check staying correct until the remaining off_t users are converted.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted six versions and answered review within a day early in the thread (message #3). No version after v6 and no reply to message #28 is visible.

priority.reason: The fix helps only Windows MSVC builds with a segment size above 1GB, but it is already committed and the rest is a small test module. A committer is engaged and has listed concrete changes, so a v7 that answers message #28 can move forward.

provisional_note: The code was not read. What v6 changes in meson.build is known only from the quote in message #28, and how the test behaves on a filesystem without sparse files could not be checked.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Windows pg_basebackup unable to create >2GB pg_wal.tar tarballs ("could not close file: Invalid argument" when creating pg_wal.tar of size ~ 2^31 bytes)
precedents_retrieved.summary: On Windows, pg_basebackup in tar mode fails with "could not close file: Invalid argument" when pg_wal.tar grows past 2^31 bytes, because off_t, lseek() and ftruncate() are 32-bit there. A proof-of-concept patch redirects lseek() to _lseeki64() so the WAL tar file can exceed 2 GiB.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last message discusses how to back-patch the fix, including an ftruncate() replacement, and nobody objects to it. The entry was withdrawn three days later, and no message gives a reason.

precedents_retrieved.title: Large files for relations
precedents_retrieved.summary: The first plan stored each relation fork as one large file instead of 1 GB segments, converted old segmented relations at upgrade and other rewrite points, and later dropped segment support. After feedback the author narrowed it to an initdb --rel-segsize option that sets the segment size per cluster, with the default unchanged.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author dropped the first plan because segmented mode cannot be removed: ext4 limits files to 16TB, and whole-relation files make file-level backups coarser. The --rel-segsize patch then missed v17 over open problems with incremental backup: pg_combinebasebackup and the segment size, and memory use in basebackup_incremental.c that grows with segment size. Peter Eisentraut's May 2024 review found that the patch needed a rebase and that pgbench/001_pgbench_with_server fails with a 64kB segment size. No revised patch appears in the visible messages.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: If I run it with 64kB, the test pgbench/001_pgbench_with_server fails consistently, so it seems there is still a gap somewhere.

precedents_retrieved.title: always use runtime checks for CRC-32C instructions
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch would always build both the CRC-32C intrinsics implementation (SSE 4.2 or ARMv8) and the fallback, and pick one through a runtime check. This would remove the compile-time-only path and simplify adding newer instructions such as ARM PMULL.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the runtime check adds a per-call cost on hardware that almost always has these instructions. Nathan Bossart's pg_waldump test showed about 0.8% slowdown from the check, and Tom Lane's buildfarm scrape showed that M-series Macs, a popular platform, would regress. The two agreed that platforms without a runtime check should use newer instructions only when the default compiler flags allow them, so the author withdrew the patch and moved the work to the original thread.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Really this just reinforces my concern that doing a runtime check all the time is on the wrong side of history.

precedents_retrieved.title: Windows filesystem support improvements
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a small C TAP framework for unit-testing low-level code without a server, plus tests of the src/port Windows filesystem wrappers. Explicitly request Windows 10 POSIX unlink and rename semantics through SetFileInformationByHandle(), based on Victor Spirin's earlier patch, with fallback code where unsupported.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew it. Explicit POSIX semantics work on NTFS, but ReFS and SMB do not support them, and nothing in CI or the build farm tests those filesystems. The tree would then gain code that breaks on them, which amounts to dropping support, and no non-POSIX code could be removed unless the project declared SMB and ReFS unsupported.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
But that would
move the traditional behaviour into a blind spot that we have no
testing for: ReFS and SMB.  Our tree would probably gain more stuff
that doesn't work on them, so that would be tantamount to dropping
support.

precedents_retrieved.title: invalid data in file backup_label problem on windows
precedents_retrieved.summary: On Windows, a backup_label file written with CRLF line endings makes recovery fail with "invalid data in file backup_label", because the parser expects '\n' after each line. The patch opened backup_label and tablespace_map in text mode when reading them, so the server would accept CRLF line endings.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The thread switched from changing the server to a documentation fix. The fix tells users to write backup_label byte for byte, in binary mode. David Steele's documentation patch was committed and backpatched as 6fb66c26, and the author agreed to write the file in binary mode, so the entry was withdrawn. The messages that argued against the server change are in the part of the thread not shown.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: It's not hurtful anywhere, there's really no reason ever to open it in text mode.

precedents_retrieved.title: pgrename_temp() – concurrent rename of temporary files on Windows
precedents_retrieved.summary: On Windows, pgrename() fails with "Permission denied" when the target file is open by another process, which breaks pgstat temporary file renames. The final patch adds a separate pgrename_temp() function that uses ReplaceFile() for non-critical files, while durable files keep using MoveFileEx().
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that a separate rename and rename_temp API makes every call site choose between them because of one platform's bugs, and that portability issues should be isolated in platform-specific files. David Steele agreed and noted that the fix could not be isolated into a Windows-specific rename(). Tom Lane added that the main motivating case, pg_stat_tmp, was expected to go away with the shared-memory stats collector.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
That's allowing a single platform's implementation
bugs to dictate our APIs globally; plus it's not clear that every
call site can know which is more appropriate.

precedents_retrieved.title: Strip Windows newlines from extension script files manually.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Strip Windows newlines from extension script files manually.
Reverted commit(s): Read extension script files in text not binary mode.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Revert commit 924e03917 in favor of adding code to convert \r\n to \n
explicitly, on Windows only.  The idea of letting text mode do the
work fails for a couple of reasons:

* Per Microsoft documentation, text mode also causes control-Z to be
interpreted as end-of-file.  While it may be unlikely that extension
scripts contain control-Z, we've historically allowed it, and breaking
the case doesn't seem wise.

* Apparently, on some Windows configurations, "r" mode is interpreted
as binary not text mode.  We could force it with "rt" but that would
be inconsistent with our code elsewhere, and it would still require
Windows-specific coding.

Thanks to Alexander Lakhin for investigation.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add timeline to partial WAL segments
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds the timeline that a promoted server switches to into the name of the .partial WAL segment it archives, for example 000000010000000100000001.00000002.partial. This prevents archive conflicts when several promotions in HA setups produce the same .partial file; prioritizing .history files in the archiver was proposed alongside it.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author stopped working on it. After discussion, Michael Paquier agreed with a revised scheme in which pg_receivewal would also use the timeline-suffixed name. The author then marked the patch Waiting on Author because it needed more work, and no new version followed for about 20 months. Robert Haas and Michael Paquier also objected to back-patching the naming change into minor releases, but that did not decide the entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: As nothing has happened here, I have marked the patch as RwF.

precedents_retrieved.title: Map WAL segment files on PMEM as WAL buffers
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patchset maps WAL segment files that live on persistent memory (PMEM) directly into memory with libpmem and uses them as the WAL buffers, so WAL is written in place without a separate copy and write. It adds a --with-libpmem build option and a wal_pmem_map setting, and sizes the mapped buffers to min_wal_size with pre-allocation by walwriter.
precedents_retrieved.objection: No reviewer took it up. Jacob Champion returned it in a batch of patchsets that did not get enough reviewer interest, and he wrote that this was not a rejection and that there was little actionable feedback. Earlier messages only asked for build fixes, CI support and rebases, and the author did each of them.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
As discussed in [1], we're taking this opportunity to return some
patchsets that don't appear to be getting enough reviewer interest.

This reverts commit 54fb8c7, as per the issues reported by fairywren

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Add missing padding from MemoryChunk struct"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Add missing padding from MemoryChunk struct"
Reverted commit(s): Add missing padding from MemoryChunk struct; Use MAXALIGN() in calculations using sizeof(SlabBlock)
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit df0f4feef.  It turns out the problem which was causing
the 32-bit ARM and PPC animals to fail was due to a MAXALIGN problem in
slab.c.  This was fixed by d5ee4db0e.  The padding that was added in
df0f4feef would only do anything on machines where uint64 was not aligned
to 8 bytes.  The 32-bit machines which were failing are not in that
category, so revert this commit.

roaster_notes.note: Neither precedent was stopped by a reason that applies to this proposal. P1 has no recorded reason, and P2 stalled on runtime segment size and incremental backup. In message #4, Thomas Munro says P2 moved from spreading pgoff_t to blocking oversized segments. That block is now committed separately (message #19), and the pgoff_t change went to HEAD only (message #24).
The C API change to pgoff_t is HEAD only and was committed without backpatching, which avoids a minor-release ABI break. The test module adds no user-facing SQL or GUC surface.
Apart from the meson check, nothing persistent changes. The on-disk format, WAL, catalogs and the wire protocol stay the same, and the fd.h ABI change is limited to HEAD, as agreed in message #2.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. It changes internal offset types and the Windows OVERLAPPED wrappers, and it adds a test module that is not installed by default and is marked NO_INSTALLCHECK. The planned File* SQL wrappers in message #28 would accept raw File numbers, but this is acceptable only while they stay in a test module that is never installed in production. Disk use without sparse files is a test infrastructure concern for PG_TEST_EXTRA, not a security one.
The I/O type change itself is committed to HEAD and was supported by Michael, Thomas and Andres, so no objection is raised against it.

No existing feature gives Windows MSVC builds correct 64-bit offsets in fd.c, md.c and the OVERLAPPED wrappers; the default 1GB segment size only avoids the bug. A committer already pushed the I/O changes. The remaining test module does not duplicate any existing test module or extension that I can name with confidence.

The demand objection does not hold. The I/O fix is committed to HEAD, and Paquier, Munro and Freund all asked for the pgoff_t cleanup and the test module (messages #2, #4, #8, #9). The remaining cost, the 4GB test on small machines, is a design point Paquier already raised (message #24).
